title: “THE OLD HAS PASSED AWAY”… SO WHY ARE YOU STILL FIGHTING THE PERSON YOU USED TO BE?
paragraphs: “THE OLD HAS PASSED AWAY”… SO WHY ARE YOU STILL FIGHTING THE PERSON YOU USED TO BE?

You gave your life to Jesus. You believed you were made new. But then the old temptations returned, the same wounds reopened, and the same sins you thought you had buried came knocking again. Does that mean your transformation wasn't real? Or have you misunderstood what God actually promised when He called you a new creation?
There is a kind of pain Christians rarely talk about.
Not the pain of being rejected by the world.
Not the pain of being misunderstood by unbelievers.
But the pain of kneeling beside your bed, asking God to forgive you for something you promised Him you would never do again.
And the worst part?
You meant that promise.
You weren't pretending when you surrendered your life to Jesus.
You weren't acting when you cried during worship.
You weren't lying when you told God you wanted to change.
You really wanted to become different.
But somehow, here you are.
Again.
The same anger.
The same lust.
The same jealousy.
The same secret compromise.
The same bitterness you thought you had forgiven.
The same anxiety that keeps you awake when everyone else is sleeping.

Maybe you haven't returned to the exact sins of your former life. Maybe your struggle is quieter now. Pride disguised as righteousness. Envy hidden beneath a smile. Resentment buried under years of church attendance.
And somewhere between another confession and another sleepless night, a terrifying question enters your mind.
If Jesus really made me new, why do I still feel so much like the old me?
That question has driven some believers into deeper dependence on Christ.
But it has driven others into despair.
Some stopped praying because they felt too ashamed to approach God.
Some stopped opening their Bibles because every verse seemed to accuse them.
Some continued attending church, singing the songs, lifting their hands, and saying all the right things while privately wondering whether their salvation had ever been genuine.
And some eventually walked away.
Not necessarily because they stopped believing Jesus could save sinners.
But because they began believing He must have grown tired of saving them.
If any of that sounds painfully familiar, stay with me.
Because there is something extraordinary hidden inside one of the most familiar verses in the New Testament.
And understanding it may change the way you see your struggle, your repentance, and the Savior who has not abandoned His people.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
Beautiful words.
Powerful words.
Words we print on Christian shirts, place on bedroom walls, and celebrate during baptism.
But what happens when the person wearing that shirt still struggles with temptation?
What happens when the person who was baptized last year falls into an old sin this year?
What happens when someone who sincerely loves Jesus discovers that becoming a new creation did not immediately remove every weakness, sinful desire, painful memory, or destructive habit?
Did Paul exaggerate?
Did Jesus fail to finish His work?
Or have we been asking this verse to promise something it never promised?
Look carefully at the original Greek.
ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις· τὰ ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθεν, ἰδοὺ γέγονεν καινά.
Hōste ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis; ta archaia parēlthen, idou gegonen kaina.
A close rendering is:
“So then, if anyone is in Christ—new creation! The old things have passed away; look, new things have come.”
Notice something important.
Paul does not say, “If anyone tries hard enough, he will eventually become a new creation.”
He does not say, “If anyone never struggles again, that proves he belongs to Christ.”
He says:
ἐν Χριστῷ — en Christō.
In Christ.
That is where everything begins.
Not in your emotional stability.
Not in your record of flawless obedience.
Not in how many consecutive days you have avoided temptation.
In Christ.
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis means “new creation.”
The word kainē emphasizes newness, and ktisis refers to creation. Paul is speaking of the astonishing reality that belonging to Christ means participating in God's new-creation work.
This is not merely a motivational slogan about improving yourself.
It is the language of divine redemption.
But there is another detail many readers miss.

The Greek verb παρῆλθεν — parēlthen, translated “passed away,” describes the passing of the old. And γέγονεν — gegonen, translated “have come” or “have become,” is a perfect-tense form pointing to a new reality that has come into being.
Paul is announcing something decisive.
Yet the verse does not say that every remaining sinful inclination has already disappeared.
And the surrounding passage tells us why.
In 2 Corinthians 5:14–21, Paul speaks about Christ dying and rising, believers no longer living for themselves, reconciliation with God, and a new way of regarding people.
The old order of alienation and living apart from Christ has been decisively confronted by His saving work.
A new relationship with God has begun.
A new allegiance has been established.
A new creation has broken into the present through Jesus Christ.
And this changes everything.
Being made new in Christ does not mean your battle with sin is imaginary. It means sin no longer has the rightful claim to rule your life.
You may still experience temptation.
You may still need to unlearn habits shaped by years of rebellion, fear, or pain.
You may still need to confess sin, seek forgiveness, repair damage, and walk through difficult processes of healing.
But your struggle must now be understood in light of your union with Christ, not as though His cross never happened.
And before anyone mistakes that for permission to keep sinning, listen to Paul's own words.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2 (KJV)
Grace is not permission to remain comfortable in darkness.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings sinners into a new life with Christ.
And genuine grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Think about Peter.
Not the stained-glass Peter.
Not the Peter whose name appears in sermons about courage.
The real Peter.
The man who had walked beside Jesus.
The man who had witnessed miracles.
The man who had boldly declared that even if everyone else fell away, he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
The fire.
The questions.
The fear.
And three denials.
Imagine the sound of that rooster.
Imagine the unbearable weight of realizing that the very mouth which had promised loyalty had now denied knowing the Lord.
Luke tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Those tears were real.
His failure was real.
And the consequences of his fear could not be dismissed as though nothing had happened.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter beside the Sea of Galilee.
There, in John 21, the risen Savior confronted the matter of Peter's love and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Jesus did not call Peter's denial obedience.
He did not pretend the betrayal was harmless.
But neither did He treat Peter's worst night as the only truth about his future.
The man who had denied Jesus would go on to proclaim Him.
Not because Peter discovered some hidden reservoir of human perfection.
But because the risen Christ is merciful, powerful, and faithful.
That is the difference between the Gospel and mere self-improvement.
Self-improvement says, “Repair yourself until you are worthy of another chance.”
The Gospel announces that Christ died for the ungodly and calls sinners to repentance, faith, and a life transformed by His grace.
And sometimes the people who most desperately need to remember that truth are the ones sitting in church every Sunday.
Because there are believers who understand that Jesus forgave their sins before conversion but struggle to believe He remains their Advocate after conversion.
They imagine that God welcomed them when they were lost but now watches their weakness with nothing but disappointment.
Yet Scripture says:
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” — 1 John 2:1 (KJV)
Read that carefully.
John's purpose is that believers do not sin.
There is no celebration of compromise here.
But he also recognizes the possibility that believers will sin.
And where does he direct them?
Not toward hiding.
Not toward pretending.
Not toward earning their way back through religious performance.
Toward Jesus Christ the righteous.
Our Advocate.
The One whose saving work is sufficient.
The One whose righteousness, not ours, is the foundation of our hope.
And here is where the story becomes even more personal.
Some of us have confused conviction with condemnation.
They are not the same.
Conviction, rightly understood, brings sin into the light and calls us toward repentance and obedience.
Condemnation declares a final verdict of guilt and punishment.
Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
That does not mean Christians never face correction, discipline, earthly consequences, or the painful responsibility of making things right.
It means those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict from which He has redeemed them.
The enemy of your soul would gladly exploit your guilt to persuade you that returning to God is pointless.
But the Gospel calls you to bring your sin into the light.
The answer to sin is not secrecy.
It is repentance.
It is confession.
It is trusting Christ.
It is walking in the light rather than making peace with darkness.
And yes, sometimes it means telling another mature believer the truth you have been too embarrassed to say aloud.
Sometimes it means ending a relationship that continually draws you into disobedience.
Sometimes it means removing access to something that repeatedly feeds temptation.
Sometimes it means seeking wise pastoral counsel, professional support, or accountability for patterns you cannot responsibly address alone.
None of those actions purchases forgiveness.
They can, however, become part of the obedient response of someone who has received grace.
Because God never called you to use your new identity as a disguise for an unchanged allegiance.
He called you to walk in the life Christ has given you.
Paul describes this tension with remarkable clarity in Galatians 5:17:
“For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other...” (KJV)
The Greek word σάρξ — sarx, often translated “flesh,” does not simply mean your physical body is evil.
In this context, Paul is describing the fallen, sinful orientation that resists the Holy Spirit.
The conflict is real.
The Spirit calls believers toward holiness.
The flesh pulls toward sinful desires.
And Paul is speaking to Christians.
Not merely to people who have never known God.
That matters.
Because the existence of conflict is not, by itself, proof that conversion never happened.
But neither should we assume that every internal conflict proves someone is saved.
Scripture calls us to examine ourselves, repent sincerely, trust Christ, and look for the fruit of His Spirit.
The question is not simply, “Do I still struggle?”
A deeper question is:
What am I doing with that struggle?
Am I defending my sin?
Am I nurturing it secretly?
Am I calling darkness harmless because confronting it would cost me something?
Or am I bringing it before God, turning away from it, and learning to obey Him even when obedience is difficult?
There is an enormous difference between a believer who falls and grieves over sin and someone who deliberately makes peace with sin while refusing Christ's call to repentance.
The difference is not that one person deserves grace more.
It is that saving faith is not indifferent to the Lord who saves.
And this is why another passage deserves your attention.
Philippians 1:6 says:
“Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (KJV)
Notice the movement.
God begins.
God continues His work.
And that work moves toward the day of Christ.
Christian transformation is not presented as a self-powered project completed the moment someone first believes.
The New Testament speaks of believers having been sanctified in Christ, being sanctified, and awaiting the final transformation that will accompany Christ's return.
Hebrews 10:14 brings the tension together:
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.” (KJV)
Christ's once-for-all sacrifice is sufficient.
And those who belong to Him are being made holy.
There is no contradiction between the completeness of Christ's saving sacrifice and the continuing work of sanctification in the believer.
Your standing before God rests upon Christ.
Your growing obedience flows from your relationship with Him.
Your final hope is the completion of His redemptive work.
And until that day, Christians are called to walk by faith.
Sometimes that walk includes victories that once seemed impossible.
Sometimes it includes painful exposure of pride you did not know was there.
Sometimes it includes discovering that a habit you thought you had conquered still requires vigilance.
Sometimes it includes the difficult work of forgiving someone who never apologized.
And sometimes it includes learning that healing from a wound and repentance from sin are not identical things.
Not every emotional struggle is evidence of rebellion.
Grief is not automatically unbelief.
Trauma is not automatically a moral failure.
An unwanted intrusive thought is not the same as choosing to entertain sin.
Anxiety or depression does not, by itself, mean someone lacks faith.
Jesus Himself wept.
Paul described affliction and weakness.
And Scripture gives us language for lament as well as praise.
We must never turn the promise of new creation into a weapon against wounded people.
Christ does not require His children to pretend they are unhurt in order to prove they belong to Him.
At the same time, suffering does not make every response to suffering righteous.
We can bring both our wounds and our sins honestly before the Lord.
He knows the difference.
And His Word teaches us to take both seriously.
Perhaps you grew up in a home where love had to be earned.
Perhaps you were constantly reminded of your mistakes.
Perhaps the people who were supposed to protect you taught you that failure meant rejection.
And now, without realizing it, you have begun imagining God through the lens of those experiences.
When you fail, you expect abandonment.
When you stumble, you expect humiliation.
When you pray, you imagine Heaven answering with exhausted silence.
But God has revealed His character most clearly in Jesus Christ.
And Jesus told a story about a son who walked away from his father.
The younger son demanded his inheritance, left home, and squandered what he had received.
Eventually, broken and hungry, he came to himself.
He rehearsed a confession.
He knew he had sinned.
He knew he had no right to demand restoration on his own terms.
And when he returned, his father saw him while he was still a long way off.
The father ran.
He embraced him.
He kissed him.
The son confessed.
And the father celebrated his return.
Read Luke 15:11–32.
The son did not discover that rebellion had been harmless.
He discovered that his father's mercy was greater than he had imagined.
That parable is not a license for believers to wander deliberately, assuming there will never be consequences.
It is a revelation of the joy of repentance and the gracious welcome of the Father.
And maybe someone reading this has been standing at a distance for far too long.
You still believe in God.
You still know the verses.
You still remember what it felt like to pray without hiding.
But shame has persuaded you that you should remain far away until you can present a better version of yourself.
Listen.
You do not clean yourself into worthiness before coming to Christ.
You come to Christ because you need the Savior.
And as you come to Him, you do not cling defiantly to the sins He calls you to forsake.
You surrender them.
You confess them.
You trust Him.
You begin again in obedience—not because His sacrifice must be repeated, but because His mercy is sufficient and His Spirit is at work.
There is something profoundly beautiful about a Christian who no longer needs to pretend.
Someone who can say, “I love Jesus, and I am still learning to obey Him.”
Someone who can confess, “I was wrong,” without collapsing into hopelessness.
Someone who can acknowledge progress without becoming proud.
Someone who can acknowledge failure without declaring the Gospel powerless.
Someone who understands that holiness is not a performance staged for an audience.
It is a life increasingly surrendered to God.
And no, that growth will not always look dramatic.
Sometimes transformation is a person who once exploded in rage choosing to remain silent long enough to pray.
Sometimes it is someone who used to lie automatically finally telling the truth, even when the truth costs them.
Sometimes it is a husband confessing his wrongdoing without blaming his wife.
Sometimes it is a wife refusing to let bitterness define the rest of her life.
Sometimes it is a young believer deleting the secret account that continually led them toward temptation.
Sometimes it is an exhausted Christian opening the Bible again after months of spiritual dryness.
Sometimes it is a person who has been hiding for years finally asking, “Will you pray with me? I need help.”
None of these things earns salvation.
But they can be evidence of grace changing the way someone lives.
And there is a passage that captures the beauty of this ongoing transformation.
“But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.” — 2 Corinthians 3:18 (KJV)
The Greek verb μεταμορφούμεθα — metamorphoumetha means “we are being transformed.”
It is a present-tense passive form.
In this context, it speaks of transformation being worked in believers as they behold the Lord's glory.
Not merely trying to manufacture holiness through willpower.
Not becoming obsessed with the old self.
But being changed by the Spirit as we turn toward Christ.
Do you see it?
The Christian life is not fundamentally about staring at your failures until you hate yourself enough to change.
It is about looking to Jesus, believing His Word, repenting of sin, and walking by the Spirit.
You cannot shame yourself into resurrection life.
That life comes through Christ.
And the same Jesus who saves you is the One who calls you to follow Him.
Not casually.
Not halfheartedly.
Not with a secret agreement to keep your favorite sins untouched.
He calls you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him.
That is costly grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that restores.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says:

“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.” (KJV)
Grace is not the opposite of holiness.
Grace trains us in holiness.

And if you are waiting for the day when following Jesus requires no struggle, no surrender, no self-denial, and no dependence upon the Holy Spirit, you are waiting for something Scripture does not promise in this present age.
One day, the struggle with sin will end for those who belong to Christ.
One day, what is perishable will put on imperishability.
One day, the people of God will be raised in glory.
One day, the work of redemption will reach its glorious completion.
But until then, we walk by faith.
We confess.
We repent.
We forgive.
We resist temptation.
We pursue righteousness.
We encourage one another.
We get up after falling—not because falling is insignificant, but because Jesus Christ is greater than our failures.
And perhaps the most important question for you tonight is not whether you have ever stumbled since becoming a Christian.
Perhaps it is whether you are still trying to live as though your past has the authority to name you.
Because your past may explain some of your battles.
But it does not have the right to overrule what God declares about those who are in Christ.
Your former sins are not a badge of honor.
Your wounds are not your entire identity.
Your failures are not your savior.
Your achievements are not your righteousness.
Jesus is Lord.
And in Him, a new creation has begun.
This is why the words “the old has passed away” are so much bigger than a promise that you will never have another difficult day.
They announce a new reality established through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
They announce reconciliation with God.
They announce that believers no longer belong to the old order in the same way they once did.
They announce a new direction, a new allegiance, and a new hope.
And they point toward the day when the new creation will be revealed in fullness.
So when the old temptation returns, do not welcome it as your master.
Resist it.
When sin is exposed, do not excuse it.
Confess it.
When you have harmed someone, do not hide behind the language of grace.
Take responsibility and seek to make things right.
When shame tells you to disappear, remember the Advocate who calls you into the light.
And when you cannot see how far you have come, remember that sanctification is not measured only by how impressive you appear to other people.
God sees the hidden acts of obedience.
The prayers nobody hears.
The apologies that cost you your pride.
The temptations resisted when nobody was watching.
The quiet surrender after a long battle with self-will.
But remember this too.
Not every struggle ends quickly.
Not every consequence disappears after repentance.
Not every relationship can be restored to what it once was.
Not every wounded heart heals on the timetable we would choose.
Christian hope does not require us to deny these realities.
It rests on the faithfulness of Jesus Christ in the middle of them.
And that is why I want to speak to the person who almost stopped reading because these words have come too close to home.
The person who has been praying the same prayer for years.
The person who is afraid that another confession will sound meaningless.
The person who has secretly wondered whether God would be better off without them.
Please hear what the Gospel actually says.
Christ did not die because sinners were already worthy.
He died for sinners.
He did not rise from the grave merely to inspire temporary improvement.
He rose in victory over sin and death.
And He does not call His people to make peace with their bondage.
He calls them into the freedom of belonging to Him.
If you are living in unrepentant sin, do not use these words to comfort yourself while refusing to turn.
Repent.
If you are crushed by guilt over confessed sin, do not treat your shame as more authoritative than the promises of God.
Look to Christ.
If you are unsure whether you truly belong to Him, do not settle for an emotional slogan or a religious label.
Turn to Jesus in repentance and faith.
If you are weary from fighting temptation, seek the help of faithful believers who will speak truth to you with love.
And if you have begun to believe that your story is already ruined beyond redemption, remember what God accomplished through the cross.
The greatest scandal in human history was that the sinless Son of God was condemned and crucified.
Yet through that very cross, God accomplished the redemption of sinners.
Human evil did not defeat His saving purpose.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, the story of everyone who belongs to Him is not finally defined by sin, shame, or death.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because every earthly consequence will vanish.
But because Jesus Christ redeems sinners and makes all things new according to His perfect purpose.
That is the message we carry at Gospel Warrior.
Not that Christians are perfect.
Not that following Jesus is easy.
Not that faith eliminates every tear.
But that the crucified and risen Christ is worthy of our complete trust, and His Word remains the foundation for genuine transformation.
If this article has uncovered something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You do not need to disclose private details publicly. God knows what those words mean.

And if you have a testimony of how Christ brought you out of a destructive pattern, consider sharing it. Not to glorify the darkness you escaped, but to magnify the mercy of the Savior who met you there.
There is someone on your Facebook friends list who may never walk into a church this week.
Someone who still believes in God but has quietly stopped praying.
Someone who thinks becoming a Christian means they should never struggle again.
Someone who has been measuring God's love by the number of times they have failed.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page, but because the Gospel is too important to keep to ourselves.
You may never know whose private prayer is answered through a truth you decided to share.
But I also want to speak about something that matters deeply to this ministry.
A message like this does not have to end when you finish reading.
It can become the beginning of deeper discipleship.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand the reach of biblical articles, Christian books, teaching resources, and encouragement for people who are hungry for the Word of God.
We want people who cannot afford expensive Christian resources to have opportunities to study Scripture, grow in discernment, strengthen their faith, and become better equipped to follow Jesus.
That work takes time, effort, and practical resources.
It is simply one additional opportunity to give generously and intentionally toward work you believe is honoring Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But willing generosity, motivated by love for Christ and concern for people who need His Word.
These products are not the reason we preach the Gospel.
You can still help meaningfully.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to read Scripture.
Encourage a struggling Christian.
Tell someone what Jesus has done for you.
Use the free resources available to you and grow in the knowledge of Christ.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
But never confuse the means with the mission.
Jesus is the treasure.
Not the platform.
Not the products.
Not the numbers.
Jesus Christ.
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who gives His people new life.
And the One who will complete His redemptive purpose.
So before you leave this article, return with me to the question that brought us here.
If the old has passed away, why am I still struggling?
Because new creation has already begun in Christ, but its full consummation is still ahead.
Because your relationship to sin has changed, even though you must still resist its influence.
Because sanctification is a continuing work of God's grace, not a declaration that you have already become incapable of sin.
Because the Holy Spirit is forming Christlike character in people who still live in a fallen world.
Because the Savior who justifies His people also calls them into a lifelong journey of holiness.
And because the final chapter of your redemption will not be written by your old nature.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
One day, the struggle will be over.
Not because you finally mastered every weakness through human effort.
But because Christ will bring His people into the fullness of the life He has promised.
Until then, do not glorify your failures.
Do not excuse your sin.
Do not worship your progress.
Do not surrender to despair.
Fix your eyes on Jesus.
When you fall, repent and return to Him.
When you stand, give Him the glory.
When you grow weary, draw near to Him.
When you experience victory, remain humble.
When you cannot understand the pace of your growth, remember that your hope is not in the perfection of your performance but in the perfection of your Savior.
And when the old life calls your name, remember whose you are.
You are not being invited to pretend the past never happened.
You are being called to live in the reality that Christ has overcome sin and death.
So come out of hiding.
Bring your failures into His light.
Lay down the excuses.
Receive His mercy.
Follow His Word.
Walk by His Spirit.
And keep your eyes on the day when faith becomes sight.
Because the greatest evidence of the Gospel is not that broken people learned to look flawless.
It is that Jesus Christ saves sinners, makes them His own, and transforms them by His grace.
The old may still whisper your name, but it no longer has the authority to write the ending of a life that belongs to Jesus.
